summary: Specifies the architecture, behavior, textual representation, and usage of IPv6 addresses of different scopes. It intentionally avoids the syntax and usage of unicast site-local addresses, per an IPv6 working group decision.

plainLanguage.summary: Some addresses only work in your room, some in your house, some everywhere. This memo explains how those ranges work.

questions: what is an ipv6 scope zone
what does the percent sign mean in an ipv6 address
what is a link-local address zone id
subtitle: How IPv6 addresses that only work within a link are told apart, using zones, zone indices and a % suffix.

tldr.problem: IPv6 has addresses that are only meaningful inside part of the network, such as link-local addresses, so the same address can exist on several links at once. A node with several interfaces needs a way to say which one it means.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines scope zones, gives each zone a node-local zone index, sets rules for sending, receiving, forwarding and multicast routing across zone boundaries, and defines the textual form of an address, a percent sign and a zone id.
tldr.outcome: It gives implementations one shared model for non-global addresses, limited to link-local and multicast scopes. It has since been updated by RFC 7346 and RFC 9844.

today: RFC 4007 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7346 and RFC 9844, so read it together with those documents. It intentionally leaves out unicast site-local addresses, which the IPv6 working group chose to deprecate.

sections.title: Why Scoped Addresses Need an Architecture
sections.content:
IPv6 builds the idea of address scope into its base design: some addresses are global, others are not (a link-local address is the example the RFC gives). RFC 3513, the addressing architecture of the time, also defined unicast site-local addresses, but the IPv6 working group decided to deprecate their syntax and usage (see RFC 3879).

For that reason this document intentionally covers only link-local and multicast scopes. It specifies the architectural characteristics, expected behavior, textual representation and usage of addresses of different scopes.
sections.plainLanguage: Some addresses are like a room number that only makes sense inside one building. This memo explains how a computer keeps track of which building a room number belongs to.

sections.title: Scopes and Scope Zones
sections.content:
Every IPv6 address except the unspecified address :: has a scope, a topological span within which it is a unique identifier. For unicast there are two scopes here: link-local (interfaces on a single link) and global (anywhere in the Internet). The loopback address ::1 counts as link-local on an imaginary link with a virtual loopback interface. Anycast addresses share the scope properties of unicast. Multicast has fourteen possible scopes, from interface-local up to global, ordered by the value of the scop subfield.

A scope zone is one connected region of topology of a given scope. A scope is a size (a link, a site), a zone is a particular instance (Alice's site or Bob's site). The zone is not encoded in the address; it is found from context such as the interface the packet uses. So two links can each hold a node with fe80::1.

Each interface is its own interface-local zone, each link is one link-local zone, and there is a single global zone. Zones of other scopes are set up by network administrators. Zones of the same scope cannot overlap, a smaller zone lies entirely inside a larger one, zone boundaries cut through nodes rather than links, and each zone must be convex from a routing perspective. Each interface belongs to exactly one zone of each scope. A zone split by a failure is still the same zone.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a street name: the same street name can exist in many towns, and you only know which one from where you are standing. A zone is the town, and the address is just the street name.

sections.title: Zone Indices Inside a Node
sections.content:
Because one non-global address can appear in several zones, and a node (a router, say) can be attached to several zones of the same scope, the node gives each zone it touches a distinct zone index. Any internal use of an address can then be qualified by that index. Zone indices are strictly local to the node: the node at the other end of a point-to-point link may use entirely different numbers. Each index should carry enough information to show its scope, so that indices of all scopes are unique within the node; how that is encoded is left to the implementation.

Nodes cannot yet discover automatically which interfaces share a zone, so an implementation must allow manual assignment. By default it should assign only a unique interface index and a unique link index to each interface. Manual configuration is then needed only when two interfaces attach to the same link or to zones of different multicast-only scopes. Because a zone lies inside larger zones, putting two interfaces in different zones of scope S forces different zones for all smaller scopes too.

Index 0 SHOULD be reserved to mean the default zone of the address's scope. An implementation should pick a default zone for each scope that has more than one choice, and allow manual override. The RFC recommends that ::1 without a zone, or with the default zone, be read as belonging to the loopback link-local zone, so a host with one non-loopback interface rarely needs to write a zone index at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Each house keeps its own list of room labels. The labels are only for that house, so another house can use different numbers for the same room, and label zero means the usual room.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Forwarding
sections.content:
When an upper-layer protocol sends to a non-global, non-loopback destination, it needs to be able to name the intended zone to the IPv6 layer. Naming only an outgoing interface would be more specific than needed when several interfaces reach the same link, so a zone index must be usable. On receipt, the zone of a non-global address follows from the arrival interface, and the IP layer is recommended to hand the correct zone indices of the source and destination to the upper layer as well.

A router forwarding a packet looks up the destination in a conceptual routing table specific to the destination's zone, which only refers to interfaces in that zone. Then it checks the source: if sending on the chosen interface would cross a zone boundary of the source address's scope, the packet is discarded. For a unicast destination it also sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable with Code 2, "beyond scope of source address". That code was unassigned in RFC 2463, and the RFC says IANA will re-assign it for this purpose.

A node that receives a packet addressed to itself with a Routing Header and more than zero Segments Left checks the next address first. If its scope is smaller than the scope of the original destination, the packet MUST be discarded. Otherwise the addresses are swapped and the forwarding rules apply again. This lets a final link-local destination know the packet began on its link.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail room never sends a letter marked for one building outside that building. If a letter would have to leave its zone, it is thrown away and the sender may be told why.

sections.title: Multicast Routing at Zone Boundaries
sections.content:
Only multicast scoped routing needs attention here, since link-local addresses need no routing and site-local unicast is deprecated. A routing protocol that finds itself on a zone boundary MUST protect inter-zone integrity and maintain intra-zone connectivity.

To keep connectivity it must build forwarding information for the global groups and for the scoped groups of every attached zone, most simply with a conceptual forwarding table per zone. To protect integrity, a router sending routing information out an interface must not include information about zones other than those assigned to that interface. The RFC's example is a router connecting Organization X (interfaces 1 to 3), Organization Y (interface 4) and Organization Z (interface 5): interfaces 1 to 3 exchange global groups and organization groups learned from interfaces 1, 2 and 3, while interface 4 and interface 5 exchange only global groups and the organization groups learned on their own interface.
sections.plainLanguage: When neighbors swap news, a company only shares its private news with its own offices. The router makes sure private news never leaks to the other companies.

sections.title: Writing a Zone: the % Notation
sections.content:
To state a non-global address without ambiguity, an implementation SHOULD support <address>%<zone_id>, where % separates the literal IPv6 address from a string naming the zone. It applies to unicast and multicast addresses of non-global scope, but not to global addresses, the loopback address or the unspecified address. The zone_id need not contain the scope, because the address already gives it, so a plain number such as 2 can stand for link index 2.

An implementation SHOULD support at least non-negative decimal integers, including the default zone, and may support other strings, such as interface names, as long as they do not clash with the delimiter. When the default zone is meant, % and the zone can be left off. A prefix puts the zone before the length, as in fe80::%2/64.

The notation MUST be used only within a node and MUST NOT be sent on the wire unless every node that interprets it agrees on the meaning. The RFC leaves out how to combine it with the URL literal format, because % is the URI escape character (a zone 1 would have to be written %251), and recommends using a hostname instead of a literal address in a URL where one is available.

The RFC's usage example: from router R1 with several point-to-point links, an administrator reaches a neighbor with telnet fe80::2%3, where 3 is the link index, because plain telnet fe80::2 cannot tell which link to use.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like writing a street name followed by the town, as in "Main Street, town 3". The percent sign is the comma between them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A limited-scope address without a zone index has security implications. For example, a link-local address cannot be used in a traffic selector of a security association set up by IKE when the IKE messages travel over global addresses, and it cannot be used in access control lists without a zone index.

The routing rules in Section 10 are guidelines for stopping zone-specific information from leaking out of its zone; if multicast site boundary routers forward site routing information outward, the integrity of the site could be compromised. The textual notation stays inside one node, so it creates no vulnerability from outside, but a malicious node could send a textual non-global address with a zone index to mislead a receiver about the zone, so implementations should be careful with such text received as data.
sections.plainLanguage: Private news must stay in its own zone, and a computer should not trust a note that claims to know which room it is meant for.

items.title: Cut through nodes
items.text: Zone boundaries cut through nodes, not links.

items.title: No overlap
items.text: Zones of the same scope cannot share links or interfaces.

items.title: Nested
items.text: A zone falls completely within zones of larger scope.

items.title: Convex
items.text: Packets between interfaces in a zone are never routed outside it.
